sections.title: Part 1 · Listening to Problem Solving
sections.instructions: Listen to the conversation and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
STYLIST: Luster Hair Studio, this is Renee.
CLIENT: Hi Renee, it's Tamsin Lowry. I have an appointment at 3 today for a cut and colour, but I just got a text saying it might be delayed.
STYLIST: I'm so sorry, Tamsin. Our colourist's previous client ran long due to an allergic reaction test that took extra time for safety reasons, so we're running about forty-five minutes behind.
CLIENT: That's a big delay. I have to pick up my kids from school at 5:30, so I can't stay too much later than that.
STYLIST: I completely understand. Given the timing, we might not be able to finish both the cut and the full colour service today. Would you like to prioritize one over the other?
CLIENT: The colour matters more to me today, I have an event this weekend.
STYLIST: In that case, I'd suggest we start the colour now if you can wait fifteen more minutes, and reschedule the cut to a separate, shorter appointment.
CLIENT: That works. Would there be a fee for splitting the service like this?
STYLIST: No additional fee, since this is due to our scheduling issue, not a choice you made. I'll also apply a ten percent discount to today's colour service for the inconvenience.
CLIENT: I appreciate that. Can we book the cut appointment now while I'm on the phone?
STYLIST: Of course, I have an opening this Thursday at 4, or next Monday at 10. Which works better?
CLIENT: Thursday at 4 is perfect, thank you.
STYLIST: Great, I'll note everything and let the colourist know you're prioritizing the colour today.

FELIX: Now that we're both working at the same office, should we try carpooling to save on gas?
AYESHA: I'd like that. My only concern is that I sometimes have early meetings that start at 7:30, earlier than your usual start time.
FELIX: That's fine, I can adjust on those days. How many days a week would this happen?
AYESHA: Maybe twice a week, usually Tuesdays and Thursdays, but it can change depending on the project.
FELIX: Let's do this: you text me the night before if you have an early meeting, so I know to be ready earlier the next morning.
AYESHA: That works well. What about driving duties? Should we alternate weeks?
FELIX: I was thinking alternating days instead, so neither of us drives for a full week straight, which can be tiring.
AYESHA: Good idea. I'll drive Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, and you take Tuesdays and Thursdays.
FELIX: Sounds fair. What if one of us has a dentist appointment or something after work?
AYESHA: Let's agree that whoever has the appointment just takes their own car that day, no hard feelings.
FELIX: Perfect. I'll message you tonight to confirm we're starting this Monday.

sections.passageTitle: City adopts four-day garbage collection trial
sections.passage: ANNOUNCER: The city council voted yesterday to launch a one-year trial reducing garbage collection from weekly to biweekly in six pilot neighbourhoods, while keeping recycling and organics collection weekly in those same areas. The change is intended to encourage composting and reduce landfill waste, following similar trials in other cities that reported waste reduction of up to twenty percent within the first year. Residents in the pilot neighbourhoods will receive a larger organics bin at no cost to accommodate the change, and the city will distribute informational pamphlets about proper composting before the trial begins next month. Some council members voted against the measure, citing concerns about odour and pest problems during summer months, when biweekly collection could mean garbage sitting out longer in warm weather. The city's waste management director acknowledged the concern but noted that participating neighbourhoods were selected partly based on having a lower proportion of homes without secure, pest-resistant bins. A public review of the trial's results is scheduled for one year from now, before any decision is made about expanding the program citywide.

WREN: Our current donor database is being discontinued by the developer in three months, so we need to migrate to something new before then.
OTIS: I've narrowed it to two options. Platform X costs eight hundred dollars a year and includes migration support, but their support team only responds within two business days.
MABEL: That's concerning if something breaks during a big fundraising push.
OTIS: Platform Y costs one thousand one hundred a year, offers same-day support, but doesn't include migration help, meaning we'd likely need to hire a contractor for that, estimated around four hundred dollars, a one-time cost.
WREN: So the first year, Platform Y would actually cost fifteen hundred total, versus eight hundred for Platform X.
MABEL: True, but in year two, without the one-time migration cost, Platform Y is only three hundred more than Platform X annually.
OTIS: Given how much we rely on the database during our fall campaign, I lean toward Platform Y for the faster support alone.
WREN: I agree the support matters, but is there a middle option? What if we use Platform X but pay extra for their premium support tier?
OTIS: I checked, and premium support for Platform X is available for an additional two hundred dollars a year, bringing same-day response times.
MABEL: That would make Platform X with premium support one thousand dollars total in year one, which is still five hundred less than Platform Y in year one.
WREN: And it includes migration support already, so there's no separate contractor cost either.
OTIS: That actually sounds like the better deal overall. Let's go with Platform X plus the premium support tier.

sections.title: Part 6 · Listening for Viewpoints

sections.passageTitle: Should companies allow anonymous employee reviews of managers?
sections.passage:
SPEAKER A: I think companies should implement anonymous review systems where employees can rate and comment on their managers. Without anonymity, many employees fear retaliation for honest feedback, so problems with poor management often go unreported until they cause serious turnover.
SPEAKER B: Anonymity does encourage more honest feedback, but it also removes accountability from the reviewer. Vague or exaggerated complaints, submitted anonymously, can be nearly impossible for a manager to respond to constructively, since they can't ask clarifying questions or understand the specific context.
SPEAKER A: That's true in isolated cases, but companies that have implemented these systems well typically aggregate feedback across multiple reviews rather than acting on any single anonymous comment, which reduces the risk of one exaggerated complaint causing unfair consequences.
SPEAKER B: Aggregation helps, but it still doesn't solve situations where a manager needs specific, actionable detail to actually improve. A vague pattern like "communication issues" doesn't tell a manager what to change.
SPEAKER A: A well-designed system could include structured questions alongside open comments, so employees rate specific behaviours, like meeting management or feedback delivery, which gives more actionable data than free-form complaints alone.
SPEAKER B: That's a reasonable refinement. I'd still want a parallel process where managers can request a follow-up conversation with HR to discuss unclear feedback, even if the original reviewer's identity stays protected.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is Speaker A's main argument for anonymous reviews?
options: Anonymous reviews are required by employment law
Managers generally prefer honest anonymous feedback
Anonymous systems are cheaper to implement than named ones
Without anonymity, employees fear retaliation, so management problems go unreported
questions.explanation: Speaker A argues fear of retaliation suppresses honest feedback without anonymity.

questions.label: Question 2
questions.question: What is Speaker B's main concern about anonymity?
options: It is too expensive for most companies to implement
It leads to too much positive feedback
It requires additional software licensing
It removes accountability, making vague or exaggerated complaints hard to address constructively
questions.explanation: Speaker B worries about unaccountable, hard-to-clarify complaints.

questions.label: Question 3
questions.question: How does Speaker A respond to the exaggerated-complaint concern?
options: Well-implemented systems aggregate feedback across multiple reviews rather than acting on a single comment
By denying that exaggeration ever happens
By proposing eliminating open-ended comments
By suggesting all complaints should be made public
questions.explanation: Speaker A cites aggregation as a way to reduce the impact of any single exaggerated complaint.

questions.label: Question 4
questions.question: What limitation does Speaker B still see even with aggregation?
options: It doesn't provide the specific, actionable detail a manager needs to improve
Aggregation is too costly to implement
Aggregation only works for large companies
Aggregation removes anonymity from the process
questions.explanation: Speaker B says vague patterns like "communication issues" don't specify what to change.

questions.label: Question 5
questions.question: What refinement does Speaker A propose?
options: Limiting reviews to once every two years
Including structured questions about specific behaviours alongside open comments
Requiring reviewers to sign their names after one year
Removing anonymity for senior managers only
questions.explanation: Speaker A suggests structured questions about specific behaviours for more actionable data.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: What additional process does Speaker B propose at the end?
options: Ending the anonymous review system entirely
Publishing all review results company-wide
Requiring managers to guess who wrote each review
Allowing managers to request a follow-up conversation with HR about unclear feedback while protecting reviewer identity
questions.explanation: Speaker B wants an HR follow-up option for managers, without revealing who wrote the feedback.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: What does the conversation suggest about the two speakers' final positions?
options: Speaker B fully rejects the idea of anonymous reviews by the end
They remain in complete disagreement with no common ground
They move toward a shared, more refined version of an anonymous review system
Speaker A abandons the idea of anonymity by the end
questions.explanation: By the end, Speaker B calls Speaker A's refinement reasonable and adds a further constructive suggestion, showing convergence.

From: A.J. Whitfield <aj.whitfield@mailhub.com>
To: Peak Fitness Membership Team <memberships@peakfitness.ca>
Subject: Cancellation fee dispute

Hello,

I cancelled my membership on July 3rd after relocating for work, providing my new lease as proof of address change, as required under section 8 of the membership agreement for relocation-based cancellations. I was still charged a seventy-five dollar early cancellation fee, which I understood should be waived for documented relocations.

Could you please explain this charge or correct it?

Thanks,
A.J. Whitfield

------------------------------

From: Peak Fitness Membership Team <memberships@peakfitness.ca>
To: A.J. Whitfield
Subject: Re: Cancellation fee dispute

Dear A.J.,

Thank you for your patience while we reviewed this. Section 8 does waive the fee for relocations, but only when the new address is more than fifty kilometres from the original club location. Your submitted lease shows an address approximately thirty-two kilometres away, which falls short of that threshold.

That said, I want to flag something: our system incorrectly calculated the distance using straight-line measurement rather than driving distance, which our own policy specifies as the correct method. Using driving distance, factoring in the lake between the two locations, your actual commute distance is approximately fifty-eight kilometres, which does qualify.

I've corrected this in our system and will process a refund of the seventy-five dollar fee within five to seven business days. I apologize for the initial error and for the inconvenience of having to raise this yourself.

As a separate note, I see your membership included a linked family add-on for your spouse. Since the primary membership is cancelled, the add-on will also end on the same date, and any prorated refund for that portion will be included in the same refund.

Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Best,
Carmen Reyes
Peak Fitness Membership Team

sections.title: Reading Part 3 · Reading for Information

sections.passageTitle: The strange persistence of the placebo effect
sections.passage:
For decades, the placebo effect has been treated mainly as a nuisance in clinical research, something to be measured and subtracted so scientists can isolate a drug's true effect. But a growing body of research suggests the phenomenon is more interesting, and more useful, than that framing implies.

The classic explanation is that patients who believe they're receiving real treatment report feeling better simply because they expect to, and expectation alone can influence perceived pain and even measurable physiological markers in some conditions. What researchers find harder to explain is a more recent discovery: in several trials, patients told explicitly that they were receiving an inert placebo, with no deception involved, still experienced meaningful symptom improvement compared to patients who received no treatment at all.

This finding, sometimes called the "open-label placebo" effect, undermines the assumption that deception is necessary for the effect to work. Researchers now suspect that the ritual of treatment itself, taking a pill at a consistent time, having a structured routine, or simply engaging attentively with a healthcare provider, may activate genuine physiological responses independent of belief in a specific mechanism.

This has practical implications that remain contentious. Some researchers argue open-label placebos could ethically supplement treatment for conditions like chronic pain or irritable bowel syndrome, where side effects of standard medication can be significant and the placebo response is unusually strong. Critics counter that formalizing placebo use, even transparently, risks normalizing treatments with no direct biological mechanism, and could complicate patients' trust if placebo use becomes a routine clinical tool rather than a research curiosity.

There is also a puzzle within the puzzle: the placebo effect's strength varies significantly by condition, culture, and even by the specific study, with pain and psychological conditions showing much larger placebo responses than conditions with more objectively measurable disease markers, like certain cancers, where placebo alone shows negligible impact. This pattern suggests the placebo response may be less a single universal phenomenon and more a family of related effects, some primarily psychological, others potentially tied to genuine, still-not-fully-understood physiological pathways.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is the main idea of the article?
options: The placebo effect is more complex and potentially useful than it has traditionally been treated in research
Placebos have been proven to have no real effect on patients
Placebos should replace all standard medical treatments
The placebo effect only works when patients are deceived
questions.explanation: The article argues the placebo effect deserves more serious consideration beyond being a research nuisance.

questions.label: Question 2
questions.question: What has traditionally been the main use of the placebo effect in research?
options: A method for testing patient honesty
Something to be measured and subtracted to isolate a drug's true effect
A primary treatment method for chronic illness
A tool for training new doctors
questions.explanation: It has mainly served as a baseline to subtract in clinical trials.

questions.label: Question 3
questions.question: What is the classic explanation for the placebo effect?
options: The effect only occurs in psychological studies
Patients feel better because they expect to, and expectation can influence perceived pain and some physiological markers
Patients are always being secretly given real medication
Doctors intentionally cause the effect through hypnosis
questions.explanation: The classic explanation centers on expectation influencing perception and some physiology.

questions.label: Question 4
questions.question: What is the "open-label placebo" effect?
options: A new type of medication with no side effects
A placebo effect that only works with deception
An effect observed only in laboratory animals
Patients told explicitly they're receiving an inert placebo still show meaningful symptom improvement
questions.explanation: This effect occurs even when patients know they're receiving a placebo, with no deception.

questions.label: Question 5
questions.question: What do researchers now suspect may explain the open-label effect?
options: The effect is entirely random and has no explanation
The ritual of treatment itself may activate genuine physiological responses, independent of belief in a specific mechanism
The placebo pills contain trace amounts of real medication
Patients are lying about their symptoms improving
questions.explanation: The ritual and routine of treatment itself may be part of the mechanism.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: What is one argument in favour of using open-label placebos clinically?
options: They eliminate the need for doctors entirely
They are proven more effective than all standard medications
They require no further research to implement widely
They could ethically supplement treatment for conditions like chronic pain, where medication side effects are significant
questions.explanation: Supporters point to conditions like chronic pain where medication side effects are a concern.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: What is a concern critics raise about formalizing placebo use?
options: It would be too expensive to implement in hospitals
It would require new government regulation to approve
It risks normalizing treatments with no direct biological mechanism and could complicate patient trust
It has never shown any positive results in any trial
questions.explanation: Critics worry about trust and normalizing treatments without a clear biological mechanism.

questions.label: Question 8
questions.question: What pattern does the article note about the placebo effect's strength across conditions?
options: It has never been measured for psychological conditions
It is identical in strength across all medical conditions
It is strongest for cancer and weakest for chronic pain
It varies significantly, with much larger responses for pain and psychological conditions than for conditions with objective disease markers
questions.explanation: The article notes stronger effects for pain and psychological conditions versus objectively measurable diseases like cancer.

questions.label: Question 9
questions.question: What conclusion does the article draw from this variation?
options: The placebo response may be a family of related effects rather than one single universal phenomenon
All placebo effects share the exact same underlying mechanism
Only psychological conditions show any placebo response at all
The placebo effect does not exist in most conditions
questions.explanation: The variation suggests multiple distinct effects rather than one uniform phenomenon.

sections.title: Reading Part 4 · Reading for Viewpoints
sections.instructions: Read the two viewpoints and answer the questions.
sections.passageTitle: Should cities prioritize bike lanes over street parking?
sections.passage:
Streets Should Move People, Not Store Cars
By Naledi Mokoena

A parking space along a busy street serves, at best, one or two vehicles a day, while that same strip of space converted to a protected bike lane can move hundreds of people over the same period. Cities that have removed street parking for bike infrastructure generally see local business revenue hold steady or increase, contradicting the common fear that fewer parking spots mean fewer customers; cyclists and pedestrians, it turns out, often visit more frequently and spend comparably over time, even if they spend less per visit. Given the urgency of reducing car dependency for both climate and public health reasons, treating street parking as an untouchable default no longer makes sense.

Parking Removal Ignores Real Constraints
By Desmond Farrow

The business revenue data Mokoena cites often comes from dense urban cores with excellent transit alternatives, conditions that don't apply to most residential streets or suburban commercial strips where a car is often the only realistic option for many trips. Removing parking in these areas doesn't create cyclists out of thin air; it simply makes errands harder for elderly residents, people with disabilities, and families doing a week's grocery shopping; none of these trips convert easily to a bike lane. A more honest approach evaluates each street's actual usage patterns and available alternatives, rather than applying a general principle uniformly across contexts that differ enormously.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is the main topic of the two pieces?
options: Whether public transit should be free
Whether electric cars should replace gas cars
How cities should design new highways
Whether cities should prioritize bike lanes over street parking
questions.explanation: Both authors debate converting street parking to bike infrastructure.

questions.label: Question 2
questions.question: What comparison does Mokoena make about space efficiency?
options: A bike lane costs more to build than a parking space
Bike lanes require more maintenance than parking spaces
A parking space is safer than a bike lane
A parking space serves one or two vehicles a day, while a bike lane can move hundreds of people in the same space
questions.explanation: She compares the low daily throughput of a parking space to the higher throughput of a bike lane.

questions.label: Question 3
questions.question: What does Mokoena say about business revenue after parking removal?
options: It always declines significantly
It generally holds steady or increases, since cyclists and pedestrians visit more frequently
It increases only in suburban areas
It has never been studied
questions.explanation: She cites revenue holding steady or increasing due to frequent visits from cyclists and pedestrians.

questions.label: Question 4
questions.question: What is Mokoena's overall argument?
options: Bike lanes are always cheaper to build than parking
All street parking should be banned immediately everywhere
Public health depends entirely on eliminating cars
Treating street parking as an untouchable default doesn't make sense given climate and health goals
questions.explanation: Her conclusion argues against defaulting to preserving parking, citing broader goals.

questions.label: Question 5
questions.question: What limitation does Farrow identify in the revenue data Mokoena cites?
options: It often comes from dense urban cores with good transit, unlike most residential or suburban streets
It was collected using flawed survey methods
It only applies to bike-specific businesses
It has never been replicated in any other study
questions.explanation: Farrow says the data's context, dense urban cores, doesn't generalize to other areas.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: Who does Farrow say is most affected by parking removal in less dense areas?
options: Business owners exclusively
Elderly residents, people with disabilities, and families doing significant grocery shopping
Only young, able-bodied commuters
Tourists visiting the area
questions.explanation: He lists these groups as most affected since biking isn't a realistic option for their trips.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: What does Farrow mean by saying removing parking "doesn't create cyclists out of thin air"?
options: Parking removal has no effect on transportation choices
Removing parking doesn't automatically make biking a realistic option for everyone
Bike lanes attract cyclists from other cities
Cyclists will simply appear once parking is removed
questions.explanation: He argues that removing parking doesn't magically make cycling feasible for all trip types.

questions.label: Question 8
questions.question: What approach does Farrow recommend instead of a general principle?
options: Evaluating each street's actual usage patterns and available alternatives
Banning bike lanes in all residential areas
Applying Mokoena's approach uniformly nationwide
Letting individual drivers vote on each street's design
questions.explanation: He recommends a context-specific evaluation rather than a uniform rule.

questions.label: Question 9
questions.question: On what point do the two authors implicitly agree?
options: Parking should always be preserved regardless of location
Context, such as density and available alternatives, affects whether removing parking makes sense
Bike lanes should never be built under any circumstances
Climate concerns are irrelevant to this debate
questions.explanation: Mokoena's argument relies partly on data from dense areas, and Farrow explicitly argues that context and density determine the right approach, suggesting shared recognition that context matters.

questions.label: Question 10
questions.question: Which best captures the fundamental disagreement between the two authors?
options: Whether cars should be banned from cities entirely
Whether bike lanes are ever appropriate in any city
Whether business revenue matters more than climate goals
Whether a general policy favouring bike lanes should apply broadly, or whether decisions should be made street by street based on local conditions
questions.explanation: Mokoena argues for a broader shift in priority, while Farrow insists on case-by-case evaluation based on local conditions.

sections.title: Writing Task 1 · Email
sections.instructions: Write an email based on the task below.

writingTask.title: Writing an Email
writingTask.scenario: You ordered custom business cards for your small business, but when they arrived, your phone number was printed incorrectly, off by one digit. Write an email to the printing company.
instructions: Explain what you ordered and what the error was.
Describe the impact this has had on your business.
Keep a polite but firm tone.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: Dear Customer Support, I am writing about order #PC-4471, a batch of 500 business cards, which arrived yesterday. Unfortunately, the phone number printed on the cards is incorrect, off by a single digit from what I submitted in my original order form, which I have attached for reference. This is a significant problem, since I've already begun distributing some of these cards at a networking event last weekend, and I have no way of knowing how many potential clients may have tried calling an incorrect number. I would like to request a full reprint of the order at no additional cost, given that the error appears to have occurred on your end rather than in my submitted files. If possible, I would also appreciate expedited shipping on the corrected batch, since I have another event coming up in ten days and would like the correct cards in hand well before then. Please let me know how quickly this can be resolved. Thank you for your attention to this matter. Sincerely, Marguerite Noel, Noel Design Studio

criteria.note: Covers every point in the task with relevant, specific detail.

criteria.note: Appropriate register for the audience and purpose.

criteria.label: Organization
criteria.note: Clear paragraphing, logical flow, and effective linking.

sections.title: Writing Task 2 · Survey Response
sections.instructions: Write a response to the survey questions below.

writingTask.title: Responding to Survey Questions
writingTask.scenario: Your children's school is deciding whether to eliminate letter grades in early elementary school (kindergarten through grade 2) in favour of narrative progress reports, or to keep the current grading system. Complete the survey explaining which option you prefer and why.
instructions: Give at least two reasons for your choice, using specific examples.
Address one possible concern about your choice and respond to it.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: I support replacing letter grades with narrative progress reports for kindergarten through grade 2. First, young children are still developing basic skills at very different paces, and a letter grade can label a child as behind before they've had a fair chance to catch up, which can affect their confidence early on. Second, narrative reports give teachers room to describe specific strengths and areas for growth, such as noting that a child excels at group discussion but needs more practice with fine motor skills in writing, detail that a single letter simply cannot capture. Some parents may worry that narrative reports are vaguer and harder to compare against expectations. This is a fair concern, but the school could address it by providing a simple rubric alongside the narrative, showing where a child falls relative to typical developmental milestones for their age, without reducing that information to a single letter. I believe this approach better supports young learners during these foundational years. Thank you for considering parent feedback on this important decision.

sections.title: Speaking Task 1 · Giving Advice
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 1: Giving Advice
speakingTask.scenario: A friend has been offered a chance to start their own business but would need to leave a stable, well-paying job to do it. Give your friend advice on how to think through this decision.
tips: Acknowledge that this is a significant risk.
Give two or three specific factors to weigh.
Help them think it through rather than deciding for them.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: This is a big decision, and I don't think there's a single right answer for everyone. I'd start by asking how much savings you'd have to fall back on if the business takes longer than expected to become profitable, since that financial cushion often determines how much pressure you'll feel early on. It might also help to ask whether you could test the idea part-time first, alongside your current job, before committing fully. I'd also think about how you'd feel in five years if you never tried, versus how you'd feel if you tried and it didn't work out, since regret sometimes points more clearly to the right choice than the practical pros and cons alone.

sections.title: Speaking Task 2 · Talking about a Personal Experience
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 2: Talking about a Personal Experience
speakingTask.scenario: Describe a time when you had to work with someone whose working style was very different from yours. Explain how you managed the difference.
tips: Set the scene briefly.
Describe the specific difference in styles.
Explain how you adapted and what the outcome was.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: A couple of years ago, I was paired on a project with a colleague who preferred planning everything in detail before starting, while I usually prefer diving in and adjusting as I go. At first, this caused some friction, since I felt slowed down and she felt I was being careless. We eventually agreed on a middle approach: spending the first day outlining key milestones together, then letting me handle the flexible parts of execution on my own. The project ended up going smoothly, and I actually picked up some useful planning habits from her that I still use today.

sections.title: Speaking Task 3 · Describing a Scene
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 3: Describing a Scene
speakingTask.scenario: Describe a busy hospital waiting room on a weekday afternoon. Include what you see and hear, and what different people in the room are doing.
tips: Use sensory details to set the mood.
Move through the scene logically.
Include contrasting emotions or behaviours among people waiting.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: The waiting room hums with a mix of quiet conversation and the occasional beep from a nearby monitor. Rows of chairs are mostly filled, some people flipping through old magazines, others staring blankly at the muted television mounted on the wall. Near the window, a mother comforts a restless toddler, while an older man sits perfectly still, hands folded, clearly anxious about his upcoming appointment. Every so often, a nurse calls a name, and the room briefly shifts as one person stands and disappears through the double doors, the tension resetting slightly for those left behind.

sections.title: Speaking Task 4 · Making Predictions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 4: Making Predictions
speakingTask.scenario: A group of hikers stands at a trailhead, looking at a map and then up at darkening clouds gathering over the mountain ahead. Predict what will happen next and explain your reasoning.
tips: Base predictions on specific details in the scene.
Use prediction language such as will likely and probably.
Structure your answer clearly.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: Given the darkening clouds and the map check, I think the hikers are probably reconsidering their planned route. They will likely discuss whether to continue toward the summit or choose a shorter, safer alternative trail instead. If the clouds continue to darken, I believe they will probably decide to turn back or take shelter rather than risk being caught in a storm high up the mountain. In the end, I imagine they'll choose caution over the original plan, and while some may feel disappointed about not finishing the full hike, most will likely agree it was the safer decision.

sections.title: Speaking Task 5 · Comparing and Persuading
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 5: Comparing and Persuading
speakingTask.scenario: Your community centre is choosing new equipment for its gym. Option A is a set of ten weight machines costing $8,000 total, appealing mainly to serious lifters. Option B is a mix of cardio equipment, mats, and resistance bands costing $5,000 total, appealing to a broader range of casual users. Persuade the board to choose one option.
tips: State your preference clearly.
Compare the two options directly.
Address a concern about your choice.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I recommend choosing the mixed cardio and resistance equipment. Our community centre serves people of all fitness levels and ages, and equipment that appeals to a broader range of casual users is more likely to see consistent daily use than machines geared mainly toward serious lifters. It's also three thousand dollars cheaper, leaving room in the budget for other community programs. Some board members might worry we'd lose the more dedicated gym-goers who want weight machines specifically. That's a fair point, but we could survey current members to see if a smaller, later addition of one or two key machines would satisfy that group without requiring the full initial investment.

sections.title: Speaking Task 6 · Dealing with a Difficult Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 6: Dealing with a Difficult Situation
speakingTask.scenario: You are sharing a hotel room with a colleague during a work conference, and you discover they've been using your toiletries and charging cables without asking. Explain what you would say to your colleague and how you would handle it.
tips: Stay calm and non-confrontational.
Explain what you would say directly but tactfully.
Suggest a practical way forward.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I would bring it up privately and casually rather than making it feel like a big confrontation. I might say, "Hey, I noticed some of my things have been used, like my charger and toiletries. I don't mind sharing occasionally, but could we just check with each other first?" I would try to assume good intentions, since it might not have occurred to them that it bothered me. If it continued after that conversation, I would be a bit more direct and perhaps suggest we each keep our own items more clearly separated in the room, like designating specific drawers or shelves, to avoid any further confusion or discomfort for the rest of the trip.

sections.title: Speaking Task 7 · Expressing Opinions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 7: Expressing Opinions
speakingTask.scenario: Some people believe that companies should be required to give employees a minimum number of paid mental health days separate from regular sick leave. Do you agree or disagree? Support your opinion with reasons.
tips: State a clear opinion at the start.
Give two or three supported reasons.
Acknowledge a counterargument and respond to it.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I agree that companies should offer dedicated mental health days. First, mental health struggles are just as real and impactful as physical illness, but many employees feel they need to invent a physical excuse to take time off for their mental wellbeing, which reinforces harmful stigma. Second, addressing burnout proactively, before it becomes severe, likely reduces long-term absences and turnover, which benefits the employer too. Some argue that this could be misused as extra vacation time, and that's a fair concern. However, this could be managed the same way regular sick leave already is, through reasonable documentation requirements for extended absences, without requiring detailed medical disclosure for occasional single days. Overall, I think normalizing mental health as a legitimate reason for time off benefits both employees and the workplaces they contribute to.

sections.title: Speaking Task 8 · Describing an Unusual Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 8: Describing an Unusual Situation
speakingTask.scenario: You see a photo of a small library housed inside an old, converted lighthouse, with spiral stairs leading up to different sections of books at each level. Describe it to a friend and explain whether you would like to visit.
tips: Describe the most distinctive features first.
Imagine what visiting would be like.
Give a clear personal opinion with reasons.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: This library looks wonderful. It's built inside an old lighthouse, with a spiral staircase winding up through several narrow levels, each apparently holding a different section of books. I imagine climbing those stairs while glancing at the shelves would feel like a small adventure in itself, quite different from browsing a flat, single-floor library. I would love to visit, especially to see the view from the top level, which I'd guess overlooks the coastline. My only concern would be whether it's fully accessible for everyone, since spiral stairs can be difficult for some visitors, but as a unique place to explore, it sounds fantastic.
